name: Limb lengthening surgery (LL)

card.summary: Cutting and gradually extending the femurs or tibias to add height; the only route to permanent added stature, but it is major surgery with months of recovery and documented complications.
card.aka: LL, leg lengthening, cosmetic stature lengthening, distraction osteogenesis
card.price: Forum posts cite roughly $6-25k in India; higher in the West
card.note: Major orthopaedic surgery: reported complications include infection, nonunion, nerve injury, joint stiffness and additional operations.

quick.overview:
Limb lengthening is an orthopaedic procedure in which a leg bone is cut and then slowly pulled apart so that new bone forms in the gap. It was developed to treat limb-length differences, deformities and dwarfism conditions such as achondroplasia, and it is also performed electively for people who want to be taller. In looksmaxxing forums it is the best-known height surgery, discussed by people who feel height limits their appearance or dating prospects.

The technique has decades of clinical literature behind it, mostly in medical (non-cosmetic) patients. Gains of several centimetres are described in clinical series, and the new bone is permanent. Forum users stress cost, months of rehabilitation and the possibility of complications, and some weigh it against other surgeries or purchases.
quick.mechanism: After the bone is cut, a week or so is allowed for early healing and the two segments are then separated at roughly a millimetre a day, split into several small steps. Soft tissue and bone regenerate in the gap, a process called distraction osteogenesis described by Gavriil Ilizarov. The bone then consolidates over further weeks or months. Devices include external frames and fixators, internal nails that are lengthened mechanically or magnetically, and combinations of the two.
quick.risks: Reported problems include pin-site and deep infection, bone that fails to heal, deformity, hardware failure, joint contractures, nerve injury and further operations. A classic Ilizarov-era paper grouped difficulties into problems, obstacles and true complications. China's health ministry banned the procedure in 2006 after serious side effects, according to one encyclopedia summary, and cosmetic limb lengthening in India has been described as high-demand and largely unregulated. Cost, long recovery and variable surgeon experience are recurring themes in forums.

lead: Limb lengthening, usually abbreviated 'LL' in looksmaxxing communities, is a surgical method that increases the length of a limb bone by cutting it and slowly separating the two ends while new bone and soft tissue form between them, a biological process called distraction osteogenesis.[1][2] For people who want to look taller it is the procedure that changes actual skeletal height: a typical elective result adds roughly 6 to 8 cm of standing height, which alters proportions, clothing fit and how tall a person appears next to others.[24][25] Orthopaedists also use it for limb-length discrepancy, deformity correction, bone defects and skeletal dysplasias such as achondroplasia.[3][4]

The modern method grew out of work by the Soviet surgeon Gavriil Ilizarov, whose circular external fixator and slow-distraction protocols made bone lengthening reliable enough for widespread use, building on earlier attempts such as Alessandro Codivilla's 1905 series, which had high rates of infection and failed healing.[1][2][26] Later techniques use internal lengthening nails, including motorised and magnetically driven ones, in place of or alongside external frames, and a procedure that once meant months wearing a metal cage has increasingly become an internal-nail operation.[1][27]

Published research is substantial for medical indications and has grown for cosmetic lengthening in otherwise healthy adults. Systematic reviews of cosmetic series report average gains in the 6 to 7 cm range, high patient-reported satisfaction, and a spectrum of complications from minor to operation-requiring.[24][25][28] Elective lengthening has also moved from orthopaedic niche to public conversation through news features, TikTok and podcasts, and on forums such as looksmax.org it is often described as the only route to stature beyond genetic potential, with the discussion centred on cost, countries and surgeons, recovery and whether the gain is worthwhile.[6][7][29][30]

paras: The surgery has three main phases: the bone is cut, a latency period of about a week allows early healing to start, and gradual distraction then separates the segments, typically about a millimetre a day delivered in a few small steps, until the target length is reached. A consolidation period follows while the regenerated bone hardens.[1] The process takes weeks to months depending on the length gained.

Patients commonly use crutches or walking aids during the lengthening and consolidation phases, and rehabilitation with physiotherapy is part of the process. Where an external frame is used, it is removed in a second operation after the bone has hardened.[2] A BuzzFeed News feature described patients walking on the day of an internal-nail operation, needing a walker for part of recovery and months of physical therapy several times a week.[29]

Gains are measured per segment. Cosmetic patients may lengthen the femurs, the tibias, or both, and published cosmetic series describe a mean gain of 6.7 cm with a range from 1.5 to 13.0 cm.[25] In the BuzzFeed feature an American surgeon said the usual ceiling with a magnetic nail is 8 cm because that is the limit of the nail.[29]

Ilizarov-type circular frames use wires and pins through the skin attached to rings and rods. Reviews describe hexapod fixators as a class of devices with six adjustable struts that allow precise multi-plane correction and are used in trauma, deformity and lengthening.[8] A 2021 controlled clinical trial in people with achondroplasia compared a rod-based monolateral fixator against a circular multi-axial system, reporting good lengthening close to plan, a mean fixation period of around 84 days and a regenerate length of about 8.5 cm in the experimental group.[9] Inflammation and irritation at pin sites and joint stiffness are among the described downsides of external frames.[2]

Implantable nails that lengthen from within the bone reduce external hardware. The Fitbone is described as a fully implantable motorised nail, associated in the literature with accurate correction, less scarring, lower infection risk and greater comfort.[1] A study of the Fitbone motorised nail in adolescents is among the clinical reports on this class of device.[31] Magnetically driven nails such as Precice are covered in their own entry. Registered post-market studies of Precice and Fitbone systems are currently under way.[10][11][12]

Reviews of cosmetic lengthening name three technique families: classic Ilizarov frames, lengthening over nail (LON), where a frame distracts the bone around a nail that is locked afterwards, and lengthening and then nailing (LATN), alongside fully motorised internal nails.[25][28] In the 2020 review the classic frame was the most used method (267 of 795 patients) and lengthening over nail the second (253), with implantable nails used in 63 patients, reflecting the period the studies covered.[25] A registered study of pain beliefs and function after cosmetic lengthening over nail is planned.[17]

The basic idea of gradual bone lengthening was proposed by Bernhard von Langenbeck in 1869, and Alessandro Codivilla published the first clinical attempt in 1905, cutting the femur and applying traction in 26 people. His results showed high rates of infection, tissue death and failed union, and the approach was not widely adopted.[1] A short report on leg-lengthening appeared in the British Medical Journal in 1951.[13]

Gavriil Ilizarov was born in 1921 and worked in Kurgan in the Soviet Union, where he developed an external fixator in the early 1950s after observing that a cut bone, carefully separated and held stable, regrew to fill the gap. He became head of the trauma and orthopaedics department in 1955, and national attention followed in 1968 when he operated on the Olympic high jump champion Valery Brumel.[26] Over the following decades he studied the method in thousands of patients, developed the circular transfixion-wire fixator and determined suitable separation rates.[1][2]

The method reached the West after the Italian mountaineer Carlo Mauri, treated by Ilizarov in 1980 for a tibia that would not heal, publicised the result. Ilizarov lectured in Italy in 1981, an association (ASAMI) formed in 1982, and the apparatus was licensed for manufacture in 1983 before the technique arrived in North America in 1986 to 1987.[26] His 'tension-stress' principle, that gradual tension stimulates new tissue growth, was documented in canine experiments and in clinical papers published in 1989 and 1990.[14][15] Callotasis, a lengthening technique using slow distraction of callus with a dynamic axial fixator, was described in 1987 in a series of 100 bones.[16] Ilizarov died in Kurgan in 1992.[26]

From the 1990s onward intramedullary devices began to replace frames in many practices. Reviewers describe nails that can correct deformity as well as lengthen,[27] and the introduction of the Fitbone motorised nail and, from 2011, the magnetically driven Precice nail made fully internal lengthening a mainstream option.[1][53] The same technology made elective height surgery more attractive to patients who would not accept a frame, and by 2022 media features described growing interest in elective lengthening, with a 2020 BBC report cited as finding that hundreds of men have the operation each year.[29]

Medical indications include congenital limb-length discrepancy, such as congenital fibular deficiency, where lengthening is one option alongside orthoses, epiphysiodesis and amputation with prosthetic rehabilitation; a review noted that amputation for severe cases showed favourable results with fewer complications than lengthening.[3] In achondroplasia, a systematic review found that vosoritide, growth hormone and limb lengthening all conferred benefits for height or growth, while long-term effects of growth hormone were unclear.[4] Lengthening is also used in children with leg-length differences and in reconstruction after trauma or infection.[33][34]

Cosmetic lengthening is performed for people of otherwise typical stature. Systematic reviews of cosmetic series describe patients averaging about 25 years of age, roughly two thirds of them male, and an operation motivated by dissatisfaction with height.[28] In India it has been described as in high demand and largely unregulated, with some patients as young as 13 or 14 and reports of complications and of surgeons understating risks; China banned limb lengthening in 2006 following serious side effects.[1] A registered study plans to assess pain beliefs and function after cosmetic lengthening over nail.[17]

BuzzFeed News profiled patients and surgeons in 2022. A 25-year-old patient who was 5 feet 7 inches before surgery described paying $75,000, and a Burbank orthopaedic surgeon who performs 30 to 40 such operations a year called the surgery life-altering; a clinical psychologist interviewed said there is no standard screening process and that she focuses on patients' expectations.[29] The same article noted that patients often keep the operation private, and that a bodybuilder and podcast host who had lengthening after a leg-length problem argued it should be as accepted as other cosmetic surgery.[29]

Distraction osteogenesis reliably produces new bone in the lengthened segment, and clinical series report the planned length being achieved in most cases.[9] A 2025 systematic review of aesthetic lower-limb lengthening covered 12 studies and 760 patients with a mean age of about 25 and found lengthening of 62 to 87 mm (average 67 mm) and patient satisfaction between 88.8 and 98 per cent.[28] The earlier 2020 review of 795 patients reported a mean follow-up of 4.9 years.[25]

Evidence specific to purely cosmetic patients is more limited than for medical indications, and published outcomes depend on the technique, surgeon and the length attempted. Lengthening of the Achilles tendon may be required alongside bone lengthening in some cases.[2] A 2025 meta-analysis of 7 studies and 489 patients compared external fixation with intramedullary nailing; it found no procedure-related deaths and lower rates of problems with nails, with external fixation satisfaction reaching 95 per cent.[35] The same review notes that a lengthening nail's length sets the typical ceiling per segment.[29]

Psychosocial outcomes are less well documented than bone outcomes. A 2024 scoping review of outcome measures in lower-limb lengthening was undertaken to inform a core outcome set, reflecting that reporting varies between studies.[36] Satisfaction figures are reported by clinical series, while the social effects people hope for, such as attention in dating or the workplace, are not systematically measured in the cosmetic literature.

A frequently cited classification separates difficulties into problems (resolved without surgery), obstacles (needing an operation to resolve) and true complications (intraoperative injuries or problems unresolved at the end of treatment).[5] In the 2020 review of cosmetic lengthening, patients averaged 0.78 problems, 0.94 obstacles and 0.15 complications each; ankle equinus was the most common problem and obstacle, and regenerate deformation and subtalar stiffness or deformity the most common complications.[25] A 2025 meta-analysis reported problems in 56 per cent of external-fixation patients and 37 per cent of nail patients.[35]

Encyclopedia summaries give approximate rates of infection (about 5 per cent), bone failing to grow in the intended direction (7 to 9 per cent), hardware failure (3 to 4.5 per cent) and improper distraction pace (about 4.5 per cent), and note that nonunion is a risk if separation is too fast.[1] Other documented issues include pin-site irritation, joint contracture, and nerve injury; experimental work found that nerves undergoing tension show changes in conduction, which is the basis of concern about stretch neuropathy.[2][18] Studies also describe soft-tissue changes in the elongating limb, and the importance of preserving blood supply and periosteum for bone formation.[14][19]

A single specialist centre in North America reported on 22 procedures referred to it for complications after nail lengthening, most performed abroad: hardware failure occurred in 23 per cent of the index operations, and malunion or nonunion in 45 per cent, mostly in the femur; the authors said all were treated successfully with no serious long-term irreversible outcomes.[37] A 2024 case report described a patient who travelled for cosmetic lengthening and had complications,[38] and a 2026 report described a rare failure of a Precice Stryde nail after cosmetic lengthening.[39] A UK paper has also discussed the burden that complications of health tourism place on the NHS.[40]

Surgeons quoted in the media attribute most complications to patients not following the rehabilitation plan, while critics argue that patients should be told that serious complications can occur even when they do.[29][1] Elective lengthening in healthy people raises an ethical question that orthopaedists debate: a 2025 survey of 496 US adults found 63 per cent considered it ethically acceptable and 70 per cent considered it equivalent to other cosmetic surgery, while 7 per cent would consider it themselves.[41]

China's health ministry banned limb lengthening in 2006 following serious side effects, according to encyclopedia summaries, while cosmetic lengthening in India has been described as high-demand and largely unregulated.[1] Magnetic nails are cleared by the US FDA as devices for lengthening indications, with the first Precice system cleared in 2011, and one encyclopedia-style summary notes a temporary suspension of the EU certificate for Precice in 2021.[53]

Cosmetic lengthening is generally not covered by insurance, and published cost reports vary with country and technique. One looksmax.org post lists external-fixator prices from about $6 to 10 thousand and internal-nail methods at roughly $12 to 25 thousand in India,[6] while a patient in the BuzzFeed feature said his operation cost $75,000.[29] Forum threads on financing the surgery are common.[42]

Published clinical work consists largely of case series, retrospective studies and a few controlled trials, mostly in medical rather than cosmetic patients. Examples include a controlled trial of a monolateral rod fixator versus a circular system in achondroplasia (14 patients, 28 segments),[9] a randomised trial of kinesiology taping to reduce lower-limb oedema during Ilizarov treatment,[20] a randomised trial of hydroxyapatite-coated pins and pin-track infection in leg lengthening for short stature,[43] and a retrospective study of limb lengthening with three-dimensional deformity correction.[21] Landmark papers on Ilizarov's method and its complications are among the most cited in the field.[5][15]

For cosmetic lengthening specifically, a 2020 systematic review in Bone and Joint Research (11 studies, 795 patients),[25] a 2025 systematic review of aesthetic techniques (12 studies, 760 patients)[28] and a 2025 meta-analysis (7 studies, 489 patients)[35] summarise outcomes; the original studies are mostly retrospective. Surveys of the public and of surgeons add attitude data,[41][44] and a content analysis of the 50 most-viewed English-language TikTok videos on height surgery (186.5 million views) found 60 per cent medically accurate, including 80 per cent of those made by health-care professionals.[45]

Registered studies include post-market evaluations of Precice nails in children and adults, a Fitbone patient-reported pain and quality-of-life study, a Google Trends analysis of public interest in limb lengthening, and a planned study of pain beliefs after cosmetic lengthening over nail.[10][12][17][22][46]

On looksmax.org and similar forums, LL is described as the only route to permanently increase height, and threads compare surgeons, countries and device types. One widely read post says external fixator procedures in India start around $6 to 10 thousand and internal nail methods run roughly $12 to 25 thousand, names surgeons and hospitals, and notes trade-offs: external methods mean more pain and scarring, internal methods cost more, and months of follow-up are needed.[6] Other users describe the surgery as costly and painful, and some weigh whether the money would be better spent on other procedures or purchases.[7]

Thread titles show the range of the conversation: debate over whether leg lengthening is the surgery that most increases dating 'SMV', whether it is the only surgery most members should consider, how to afford it, what the risks are, and whether a one-to-two-inch gain is realistic.[42][47][48][49] Others discuss the interaction between lengthening and later muscle development.[50]

A 2025 qualitative study in Sociology of Health and Illness analysed 8,072 comments on a looksmaxxing board with about 6 million monthly visitors. The authors, Michael Halpin and colleagues, reported that the community pushes men toward major bodily changes such as leg-lengthening surgery and mewing, and concluded that such communities can harm participants' health.[51] Reporting in the technology press has also tracked public interest: Hacker News threads on lengthening drew hundreds of comments in 2022.[52]

timeline.event: Bernhard von Langenbeck proposes gradual bone lengthening.[1]
Alessandro Codivilla publishes the first clinical series of femur lengthening with traction, with high complication rates.[1]
Gavriil Ilizarov begins developing the circular external fixator in Kurgan, USSR.[26]
Ilizarov treats Olympic high jumper Valery Brumel, bringing national fame.[26]
Italian mountaineer Carlo Mauri is treated by Ilizarov, opening the method to the West.[26]
Ilizarov method reaches US medicine; callotasis series published.[16][26]
Ilizarov's tension-stress papers and the classification of problems, obstacles and complications published.[14][5][15]
China's health ministry bans limb lengthening after serious side effects.[1]
Magnetically driven Precice nail introduced clinically, making internal lengthening mainstream.[27]
Systematic review of 795 cosmetic stature lengthening patients published in Bone and Joint Research.[25]
BuzzFeed News feature on the growth of elective lengthening draws hundreds of comments on Hacker News.[29][52]
Systematic review and meta-analysis of cosmetic lengthening appear, alongside studies of TikTok content and public attitudes.[28][35][41][45]

lore.intro: In looksmaxxing communities LL is treated as the definitive but costly height intervention, with discussion about where to have it done, which technique to choose and whether it is worth the recovery.[6][7]

claims.claim: LL is the only way to gain real, permanent height after growth plates close.
claims.believers: Forum posts present it as the 'only real option' for adults who want to be taller and as the entry point to 'heightmaxxing'.[6]
claims.experts: Orthopaedic literature documents gradual lengthening producing new bone in the segment, with clinical series reporting planned lengths achieved, mostly in medical patients.[9]

claims.claim: India is the cheapest 'legit' place to have LL done.
claims.believers: One post lists external-fixator prices from about $6 to 10 thousand and internal-nail methods from $12 to 25 thousand in India, naming hospitals and surgeons and describing quality as below top Western centres.[6]
claims.experts: Encyclopedia sources describe cosmetic limb lengthening in India as high-demand and largely unregulated, with reports of complications and understated risks.[1]

claims.claim: Internal nails give a smoother recovery than external frames.
claims.believers: Users describe external methods as causing more pain and scarring and internal ones as costlier but smoother.[6]
claims.experts: The literature associates fully implantable nails with accurate correction, less scarring, lower infection risk and greater comfort, while external frames carry pin-site irritation and contracture risks.[1][2]

claims.claim: LL is a major life-changing upgrade for dating and status.
claims.believers: Posters describe height as a persistent limitation even after other looksmaxxing and weigh surgery against other spending; others say they have seen shorter men do well after surgery.[7]
claims.experts: No study identified for this article measures dating or social outcomes after cosmetic lengthening; research on psychosocial outcomes in cosmetic lengthening is limited.

claims.claim: Complications mostly occur when patients overreach or skip rehab.
claims.believers: A surgeon quoted by BuzzFeed News says most of his patients have no complications and attributes problems to not following instructions or therapy and to attempting more than about 8 cm.[29]
claims.experts: A specialist-centre series of referred cases reported hardware failure in 23 per cent and malunion or nonunion in 45 per cent of index operations, mostly done abroad, and a systematic review recorded problems in a large share of patients.[37][25]

claims.claim: LL is dangerous and often goes wrong.
claims.believers: One post notes that external methods involve more pain and scarring and that patients abroad must stay for months of physiotherapy and follow-up, with aftercare falling to them after returning home.[6]
claims.experts: Clinical papers report infection, nonunion, nerve and joint problems and re-operations, and a classification system exists to grade them; China banned the procedure in 2006 after serious side effects.[5][1]

claims.claim: A 'lengthening then nailing' or internal-nail route avoids the downsides of frames.
claims.believers: Forum posts describe internal-nail methods as costlier but smoother than external frames.[6]
claims.experts: A 2025 meta-analysis found fewer problems with intramedullary nailing than external fixation (37 versus 56 per cent), though both groups had obstacles in 42 to 48 per cent.[35]

claims.claim: Social media shows an accurate picture of the surgery.
claims.believers: Surgeons and patients post recovery content, and many videos present education about techniques and risks.[45]
claims.experts: A study of the 50 most-viewed TikTok videos found 60 per cent medically accurate overall and 80 per cent of health-professional videos accurate, with 24 per cent raising concerns about pain or permanent injury.[45]

claims.claim: The social payoff justifies the surgery.
claims.believers: Patients quoted in the media report being treated with more respect, and forum users call it a life-changing upgrade.[29][7]
claims.experts: Research on height and social outcomes is distinct from lengthening studies, and a clinical psychologist interviewed by BuzzFeed said therapy and screening focus on whether expectations are realistic; the 2025 sociology study describes communities that push men toward surgery and links this to harm.[29][51]

claims.claim: Growth factors and peptides could improve LL results.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread titled as a theory asks whether growth factors and peptides could improve lengthening results.[23]
claims.experts: No published human trial identified for this article tests such add-ons in cosmetic lengthening.

angle.text: Lengthening of the femurs, tibias or both adds real skeletal height, typically around 6 to 8 cm in cosmetic series, which changes stature, leg proportions and how clothes fit. People pursue it when height is the feature they most want to change.
